Question: Equiangular hexagon \(ABCDEF\) has side lengths \[AB=CD=EF=1\] and \[BC=DE=FA=r.\] The area of \(\triangle ACE\) is \(70\%\) of the area of the hexagon. What is the sum of all possible values of \(r?\)
Solution:
Because \(r\) is a side length, \(r>0\). Each interior angle of the equiangular hexagon is \((6-2)180^\circ/6=120^\circ\), so each exterior turn is \(60^\circ\). This suggests extending alternating sides to create equilateral triangles.

Extend the lines \(AB,CD,EF\). Let their pairwise intersections be \(P=AB\cap CD\), \(Q=CD\cap EF\), and \(R=EF\cap AB\). These form an equilateral triangle around the hexagon. The removed corner triangles \(PBC,QDE,RFA\) each have two angles of \(180^\circ-120^\circ=60^\circ\), so they are equilateral of side \(r\). Each side of the outer triangle consequently consists of lengths \(r,1,r\), giving total length \(1+2r\).

An equilateral triangle of side \(s\) has height \(\sqrt3s/2\), by bisecting it and applying the Pythagorean theorem. Put \(K=\sqrt3/4\), so its area is \(Ks^2\). The hexagon's area \(H\) is therefore
\[
H=K\bigl((1+2r)^2-3r^2\bigr)
=K(r^2+4r+1).
\]
Triangles \(ABC\) and \(PBC\) have bases on the same line and share the altitude from \(C\). That altitude is \(\sqrt3r/2\), so \([ABC]=Kr\). The same reasoning gives \([CDE]=[EFA]=Kr\). Removing these three triangles from the hexagon leaves \(\triangle ACE\), whose area is
\[
T=H-3Kr=K(r^2+r+1).
\]
Since \(H>0\), the given percentage is equivalent to
\[
\frac{r^2+r+1}{r^2+4r+1}=\frac7{10}.
\]
Cross-multiplication and simplification give
\[
r^2-6r+1=0,
\qquad
(r-3)^2=8,
\qquad
r=3\pm2\sqrt2.
\]
Both roots are positive because \(2\sqrt2<3\). Both are realizable: for any \(r>0\), cutting equilateral corners of side \(r\) from an equilateral triangle of side \(1+2r\) leaves the required hexagon. Thus all possible values have sum \(\boxed{6}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
